stem: Patient who drinks alcohol presents with epigastric pain on and off for months; normal investigations except mildly raised AST. Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: epigastric pain on and off for months
why_right: This recall's key is cholecystitis, reading the intermittent (on and off) epigastric pain over months as recurrent biliary pain from chronic gallbladder disease, with only a mildly raised AST and otherwise normal results. Chronic cholecystitis is a recurrent, low grade process that can present this way between attacks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chronic pancreatitis: alcohol is its commonest cause and it gives recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back; it is clinched by steatorrhea, diabetes or pancreatic calcification on imaging, none of which is described here.
C. PUD: epigastric pain linked to meals (better with food in duodenal, worse with food in gastric ulcer), often with NSAID or H. pylori history; it does not raise AST.
key_concept:
Chronic epigastric pain in a drinker: look for the discriminating clue.
  • Pain radiating to the back, steatorrhea, diabetes, calcification: chronic pancreatitis
  • Meal related pain, NSAIDs, H. pylori: PUD
  • Postprandial RUQ/epigastric pain, gallstones on ultrasound: biliary disease
  • AST:ALT about 2:1 in a drinker: alcoholic liver injury
  • Chronic pancreatitis test: CT abdomen
exam_pearl: In chronic epigastric pain, the discriminating clue (back radiation and steatorrhea, meal relation, or gallstones on ultrasound) decides the answer, not the alcohol history alone.

stem: First presentation of hepatitis C virus infection found to have viral load 2 million copies. What further?
key_concept:
Confirmed HCV viremia: stage the liver, screen for coinfection, then treat with DAAs.
  • Anti HCV positive, RNA negative: no further testing (cleared)
  • RNA positive: chronic infection, treat all viremic patients
  • Baseline: genotype (if regimen needs it), fibrosis staging by Fibroscan, HBV (HBsAg, anti HBc) and HIV screening
  • Treatment: DAAs (e.g. ledipasvir/sofosbuvir for genotype 4); interferon is obsolete
  • Lead in 'stage the disease' = Fibroscan; 'risk before DAA' = HBV screening
exam_pearl: Both are standard baseline steps; read whether the stem is asking about liver staging or about DAA safety.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Lady with trigeminal neuralgia and weakness of UL. Investigation?
why_right: Trigeminal neuralgia with an additional neurological deficit (upper limb weakness) is not classical idiopathic neuralgia; it suggests a structural or demyelinating cause such as multiple sclerosis or a posterior fossa/brainstem tumour. MRI with gadolinium is the investigation of choice because it shows demyelinating plaques, active (enhancing) lesions and small brainstem or cerebellopontine angle masses that CT misses.
why_wrong_block: A. CT scan: poor at imaging the brainstem, posterior fossa and white matter, so it misses MS plaques and small lesions; it is the first test only for acute trauma or suspected hemorrhage.
key_concept:
Trigeminal neuralgia with red flags needs contrast MRI.
  • Red flags: neurological deficit, sensory loss, young age, bilateral pain
  • Young woman with TN plus other deficits: think MS
  • MRI shows plaques; gadolinium shows active lesions and tumours
  • CT: acute bleed or trauma, not demyelination
  • Classical TN with normal exam: carbamazepine first line
exam_pearl: Trigeminal neuralgia plus ANY focal deficit = secondary cause until MRI proves otherwise.

stem: Hepatic encephalopathy: what is increased?
why_right: In hepatic encephalopathy the failing liver (and portosystemic shunting) cannot convert gut derived ammonia to urea, so ammonia rises in the blood and acts as a neurotoxin, causing confusion and asterixis. This is why treatment (lactulose, rifaximin) aims to reduce ammonia production and absorption.
why_wrong_block: B. Uraemia: urea is made by the liver, so liver failure tends to lower urea; a high urea causes uraemic encephalopathy in renal failure, which is a different condition.
key_concept:
Hepatic encephalopathy = ammonia toxicity from liver failure.
  • Signs: confusion, asterixis (flapping tremor), altered sleep
  • Precipitants: GI bleed, infection (SBP), constipation, sedatives, electrolyte disturbance
  • Treatment: lactulose (enema if unable to take orally), rifaximin; treat the precipitant
  • SBP plus encephalopathy: lactulose plus IV ceftriaxone
exam_pearl: Liver failure: ammonia up, urea down; kidney failure: urea up.

stem: A patient came from Sudan 10d ago with fever rigors ..etc you are suspecting malaria which of the following drug therapy you would give him?
why_right: Fever and rigors 10 days after coming from Sudan is falciparum malaria until proven otherwise, since P. falciparum is the dominant species there. African falciparum is resistant to chloroquine, so first line treatment is artemisinin based combination therapy (e.g. artemether lumefantrine) for uncomplicated disease; severe malaria starts with IV artesunate, then completes a full ACT course.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chloroquine: right only for chloroquine sensitive species (vivax, ovale, malariae) or sensitive regions; African falciparum is resistant.
B. Quinine: an older second line alternative (with doxycycline or clindamycin) used when artemisinins are unavailable; less effective and more toxic (cinchonism, hypoglycemia, arrhythmia).
key_concept:
Falciparum malaria: artemisinins first.
  • Sudan or sub Saharan Africa plus fever: think P. falciparum
  • Diagnosis: thick and thin blood smears, repeated if negative
  • Uncomplicated falciparum: ACT (artemether lumefantrine)
  • Severe malaria: IV artesunate, then oral ACT
  • Vivax/ovale: chloroquine (where sensitive) plus primaquine for liver stage (check G6PD)
  • Prophylaxis for Africa: atovaquone/proguanil, not chloroquine
exam_pearl: Fever after travel from Sudan = falciparum = ACT; chloroquine is never the answer for African falciparum.

stem: 22-year-old man known case with AIDS on active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) presented with history of headache and weakness at left side of the body. On examination, he is found to have left hemiparesis, hemianopia, aphasia, ataxia, and 6/7 cranial nerve palsies. Investigation showed a rising titers of anti-toxoplasma immunoglobulin G (IgG) antibodies and positive immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibody. Brain MRI scans demonstrated multiple hypodense lesions in white matter and basal ganglia with mass effects. Which of the following is the best treatment option?
highlight_terms_source: multiple hypodense lesions in white matter and basal ganglia with mass effects
why_right: An AIDS patient with focal deficits (hemiparesis, hemianopia, aphasia, ataxia), rising anti-toxoplasma IgG with positive IgM and multiple lesions with mass effect in white matter and basal ganglia has cerebral toxoplasmosis. First-line treatment is pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine, given with folinic acid (leucovorin) to protect the marrow from pyrimethamine. Being on HAART does not exclude it; adherence or immune recovery may be incomplete.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rifampicin and cefuroxime have no activity against Toxoplasma gondii; this pairing targets bacteria (rifampicin is used for TB or staphylococcal infections), not a protozoal brain infection.
B. Clindamycin can replace sulfadiazine in a sulfa-allergic patient, but only when paired with pyrimethamine. Doxycycline plus clindamycin is not a toxoplasmosis regimen.
C. Leucovorin is part of the regimen only as marrow protection alongside pyrimethamine. Chloramphenicol is an antibacterial with no role in toxoplasmosis.
key_concept:
AIDS + multiple ring/hypodense lesions with mass effect + positive toxoplasma serology = cerebral toxoplasmosis.
  • First line: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin
  • Sulfa allergy: pyrimethamine + clindamycin
  • Then secondary prophylaxis until immune recovery
  • No response to empiric therapy, or a single lesion: think CNS lymphoma (EBV in CSF, biopsy)
  • Prophylaxis at low CD4: TMP-SMX
exam_pearl: Leucovorin in an option does not make it right; it only accompanies pyrimethamine.

stem: A patient admitted with heart failure The Doctors put him on sacubitril/valsartan, Spirono, Metoprolol and discharge, on follow up he's fully normal, asymptomatic, but the lab showed HYPERKALEMIA (it was mild elevation MAYBE 6) What to do. It Was 5.6, Not "6"
why_right: The patient is asymptomatic on guideline therapy for HFrEF (ARNI, MRA, beta blocker) and has mild hyperkalemia (5.6). The mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone) is the drug most likely to raise potassium, so the usual step is to reduce its dose and recheck potassium. This keeps all the mortality-reducing drugs going rather than stopping one.
why_wrong_block:
A. Option not recalled. Things a student might weigh here: stopping spironolactone completely, which is kept for higher or persistent potassium, or emergency treatment (calcium, insulin with dextrose), which is for severe hyperkalemia or ECG changes, not an asymptomatic 5.6.
B. Sacubitril/valsartan reduces mortality and contributes less to potassium than spironolactone. Stopping it for mild asymptomatic hyperkalemia removes key HF therapy; it is reconsidered only if hyperkalemia or kidney function worsens despite adjusting the MRA.
D. Option not recalled. Stopping metoprolol would not help: beta blockers are not the cause here and are mortality-reducing in HFrEF.
key_concept:
Mild hyperkalemia on HFrEF therapy: adjust the MRA first, keep the other disease-modifying drugs.
  • Mild rise, asymptomatic: reduce spironolactone dose, recheck potassium and creatinine
  • Higher or persistent rise: stop the MRA
  • Severe or ECG changes: emergency treatment (calcium, insulin with dextrose)
  • Mortality-reducing HFrEF drugs: ACEI/ARB/ARNI, beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
exam_pearl: Do not stop a mortality-reducing drug for a mild lab change when a dose reduction will do.

stem: A patient with Methamphetamine abuse, present with dehydration, dry mucus membrane, AMS, There are other symptoms but i dont remember it but for sure No Jaundice, No Lower limb edema Vital: BP: mild hypertension (forgot the number) No labs at all What's explain the patient symptoms?
highlight_terms_source: No Jaundice, No Lower limb edema
key_concept:
Methamphetamine toxicity with dehydration and AMS: match the option to the supporting clues.
  • Jaundice, asterixis, coagulopathy: liver failure
  • Oliguria, high creatinine, dark urine with high CK: kidney injury (often rhabdomyolysis)
  • Dehydration with abnormal sodium and no organ failure signs: electrolyte disturbance
  • Stimulant toxicity: also check temperature, CK, glucose
exam_pearl: Stated negatives (no jaundice, no edema) are there to be used: check which option they rule against.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 25-year-old male with chronic use of a steroid inhaler due to poorly controlled asthma presents now with a white patch on his tongue and mouth. What is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: chronic use of a steroid inhaler
white patch on his tongue and mouth
why_right: A white patch on the tongue and mouth in someone on chronic inhaled steroids is oral candidiasis (thrush), a well-known local side effect of ICS. Uncomplicated oral thrush is treated topically, and nystatin suspension is the classic topical antifungal. Advise rinsing the mouth after each inhaler dose and using a spacer to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong_block:
B. Itranidazole (likely meaning itraconazole) is a systemic azole. It is kept for refractory, severe, or esophageal candidiasis, not first-line for simple oral thrush.
C. Mebendazole is an anthelmintic for worm infections and has no antifungal action.
D. Amphotericin B is for invasive or life-threatening systemic fungal infections. It is far too toxic for local oral thrush.
key_concept:
ICS + white wipeable oral plaques = oral candidiasis; treat topically first.
  • Mild oral thrush: nystatin suspension (or clotrimazole)
  • Moderate to severe or refractory: oral fluconazole
  • Esophageal candidiasis: systemic azole
  • Invasive candidiasis: echinocandin or amphotericin B
  • Prevention: rinse mouth after ICS, use a spacer
exam_pearl: A white patch that does NOT wipe off suggests leukoplakia, not thrush.

stem: Pt with tumor lysis. Has muscle weakness, fatigue palpitations K:6.2 I cant remember the values of uric acid, Po4 and Ca His symptoms are due to;
why_right: Tumor lysis releases intracellular potassium, and this patient has K 6.2. His symptoms (muscle weakness, fatigue, palpitations) are the typical picture of hyperkalemia, which affects muscle and the heart's conduction and can cause arrhythmias. The other TLS abnormalities produce different symptoms.
why_wrong_block:
B. Hypocalcemia does occur in TLS, because phosphate binds calcium, but it presents with neuromuscular irritability: perioral tingling, cramps, tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau signs, seizures. Weakness with palpitations and a known K 6.2 points to potassium instead.
C. Hyperphosphatemia is mostly silent on its own. Its effects come indirectly through hypocalcemia and calcium phosphate deposition in the kidneys (AKI), not weakness and palpitations.
key_concept:
TLS pattern: high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, low calcium.
  • High K: weakness, palpitations, arrhythmias (most dangerous)
  • Low Ca: tetany, paresthesia, seizures, prolonged QT
  • High phosphate: renal calcium phosphate deposition
  • High uric acid: urate nephropathy, AKI
  • Prevent with hydration + allopurinol; rasburicase for high risk
exam_pearl: Match symptoms to the electrolyte: weakness/palpitations = potassium; tingling/tetany = calcium.

stem: Patient on .3 norepinephrine Hypotensive what to add?
why_right: In shock (classically septic shock) that remains hypotensive on norepinephrine at a moderate dose such as 0.3, current sepsis guidance suggests adding vasopressin rather than escalating norepinephrine further. Vasopressin acts through a separate, non-adrenergic receptor, so it raises MAP while sparing catecholamine dose and its toxicity.
why_wrong_block: A. Raising norepinephrine further increases adrenergic side effects (tachyarrhythmias, myocardial and peripheral ischemia) with less added benefit. Titrating norepinephrine is right while the dose is still low; once a moderate dose fails, add a second agent.
key_concept:
Vasopressor ladder in septic shock (after adequate fluids):
  • 1st: norepinephrine, titrated to MAP ≥ 65
  • Inadequate MAP on moderate dose: add vasopressin
  • Still inadequate: add epinephrine
  • Ongoing vasopressor need: add IV hydrocortisone
  • Cardiac dysfunction with low output: consider dobutamine
exam_pearl: Second vasopressor in septic shock = vasopressin; epinephrine comes after that.

stem: 54-year-old male with history of DM and CKD, recently admitted for acute coronary syndrome, presents to clinic for follow-up. He has high creatinine, slightly high cholesterol, low HDL, and high LDL. Which of the following medications should be added to his regimen?
why_right: A recent acute coronary syndrome means clinical ASCVD, and every such patient needs a high-intensity statin whatever the baseline LDL, especially with diabetes and CKD adding risk. Atorvastatin is a high-intensity statin with mainly hepatic clearance, so it suits a patient with high creatinine.
why_wrong_block:
B. Niacin raises HDL but has shown no cardiovascular outcome benefit added to statins. It causes flushing and worsens glucose control in a diabetic.
C. Ezetimibe is an add-on when LDL stays above target despite a maximally tolerated statin. It is not the first drug after ACS.
D. Doing nothing is wrong: post-ACS secondary prevention requires a high-intensity statin regardless of how high the cholesterol is.
key_concept:
Clinical ASCVD (MI, ACS, stroke/TIA, PAD) = high-intensity statin regardless of LDL.
  • High intensity: atorvastatin or rosuvastatin at high dose
  • LDL still above target on max statin: add ezetimibe
  • Then: PCSK9 inhibitor
  • Niacin and fibrates: no first-line role in secondary prevention
exam_pearl: Low HDL tempts you toward niacin; the outcome-proven drug is still a statin.

stem: Elderly with DM, HTN, AF, admitted for TIA. Most appropriate treatment?
why_right: AF with a TIA means a cardioembolic event has already happened. Adding elderly age, DM and HTN gives a high CHA2DS2-VASc score (TIA alone scores 2). Long-term oral anticoagulation is the treatment that prevents stroke here, with a DOAC usually preferred over warfarin.
why_wrong_block:
B. Diabetes control matters for vascular risk overall but does not prevent cardioembolic stroke from AF. It is not the most appropriate treatment for this admission.
C. Uric acid-lowering drugs are for gout or urate complications; nothing in the stem points to them.
D. A beta blocker is for rate control when AF has a rapid ventricular rate. It does not reduce stroke risk; anticoagulation does.
key_concept:
AF stroke prevention by CHA2DS2-VASc:
  • C: heart failure (1); H: hypertension (1); A2: age ≥ 75 (2); D: diabetes (1)
  • S2: prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2); V: vascular disease (1); A: age 65-74 (1); Sc: female (1)
  • Score ≥ 2 (men): anticoagulate
  • DOAC preferred; warfarin for mechanical valves or moderate-severe mitral stenosis
  • Aspirin is not adequate AF stroke prevention
exam_pearl: Rate control treats symptoms; only anticoagulation prevents the AF stroke.

stem: 30-year-old man, smoker, newly diagnosed COPD. Normal vitals, only chronic cough. Next management step?
why_right: In a smoker with newly diagnosed COPD, normal vitals and only a chronic cough, the first management step is smoking cessation. It is the single intervention that slows FEV1 decline and reduces mortality. Drugs are added according to symptoms and exacerbations.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ipratropium is given inhaled, not orally. Bronchodilators relieve dyspnea but come after quitting smoking; they would be right as symptomatic therapy or in an acute exacerbation.
C. Steroids are not initial COPD therapy. Inhaled steroids are added later for frequent exacerbations or high eosinophils; systemic steroids are for acute exacerbations. This patient is stable.
key_concept:
COPD: smoking cessation first, then treat by symptoms and exacerbations.
  • Mortality benefit: smoking cessation, long-term oxygen when hypoxemic
  • Maintenance: LAMA or LABA, then LABA + LAMA
  • ICS: add for frequent exacerbations with high eosinophils
  • Also: vaccines, pulmonary rehabilitation
  • COPD at a young age: check alpha-1 antitrypsin
exam_pearl: Words like "initial" or "next step" in a smoker with COPD point to smoking cessation, not a drug.

stem: Patient had an episode of unprovoked deep vein thrombosis. He has no personal or family history of related diseases. He has been on warfarin for three months and is tolerating it very well. His current INR is 2.5. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
OptB: Continue warfarin for total of six 6 months
OptD: Discontinue warfarin and perform thrombophilia testing
key_concept:
Duration of anticoagulation is set by whether the VTE was provoked.
  • Provoked by transient factor: 3 months, then stop
  • First unprovoked proximal DVT/PE: at least 3 months, then consider extended (indefinite) if bleeding risk acceptable
  • Recurrent VTE: long term / lifelong
  • Active cancer: continue while cancer active
  • Warfarin target INR 2 to 3
A near-identical recall of this question is keyed to Continue warfarin indefinitely.
exam_pearl: 'Unprovoked' plus 'tolerating well' points to extended therapy; 'after surgery' or 'cast' points to 3 months and stop.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Near-identical recall 1752 on the next page marks C.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: (40 or 50) patient had an episode of unprovoked (PROXIMAL or POPILITEAL) deep vein thrombosis. He has no personal or family history of related diseases. He has been on warfarin for three months and is tolerating it very well. His current INR is 2.5. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
OptB: Continue warfarin for total of six 6 months
OptD: Discontinue warfarin and perform thrombophilia testing
why_right: The DVT is unprovoked and proximal, the patient has completed 3 months of warfarin, is tolerating it very well and is therapeutic (INR 2.5), so bleeding risk is acceptable. After a first unprovoked proximal DVT the recurrence risk stays high once anticoagulation stops, so current guidance favours extended (indefinite) anticoagulation with periodic review.
why_wrong_block:
A. Stopping at 3 months suits a DVT provoked by a transient, removed risk factor (surgery, immobilisation, cast); this one was unprovoked.
B. A fixed 6 month course is the older rule for unprovoked DVT still found in some notes; it leaves an unprovoked patient with low bleeding risk exposed to recurrence once therapy stops.
D. Routine thrombophilia testing is not recommended after unprovoked VTE because it rarely changes management, and stopping effective warfarin just to test exposes him to recurrence.
key_concept:
Anticoagulation duration depends on the trigger.
  • Provoked (transient factor): 3 months
  • First unprovoked proximal DVT/PE: extended / indefinite if bleeding risk acceptable
  • Recurrent VTE: lifelong
  • Active cancer: while cancer active
  • Target INR 2 to 3
exam_pearl: Same stem with 'after surgery' or 'leg in cast' flips the answer to stopping at 3 months.

stem: HBV
why_right: For chronic hepatitis B needing treatment, the first-line drugs are the high-barrier oral nucleos(t)ide analogues: entecavir or tenofovir. They are well tolerated, potently suppress HBV DNA and have very low resistance rates, so entecavir is the expected answer when the recall just says 'HBV treatment'.
why_wrong_block: B. Pegylated interferon is an alternative only in selected patients (young, compensated liver, wanting a finite course) and has many side effects; it is contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis and pregnancy. Plain interferon is no longer first line.
key_concept:
Chronic HBV first line: entecavir or tenofovir (oral, high barrier to resistance).
  • Pregnancy / high viral load in third trimester: tenofovir
  • Renal or bone concerns: entecavir or tenofovir alafenamide
  • Lamivudine / adefovir: no longer first line (resistance)
  • Peg-interferon: finite course, selected compensated patients
  • Acute flare in chronic HBV with low DNA: think hepatitis D, check anti-delta
exam_pearl: If the options include tenofovir and the patient is pregnant, tenofovir beats entecavir.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Room with sudden onset of shortness of breath associated with pleuritic chest pain. Her past medical history is unremarkable. She is using oral contraceptives regularly. Physical examination is unremarkable. Imaging and laboratory tests are requested. Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to establish the diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: sudden onset of shortness of breath
why_right: Sudden dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain in a young woman on oral contraceptives (an estrogen related clot risk) is pulmonary embolism until proven otherwise. The lead in asks for the test that establishes the diagnosis: CT pulmonary angiography directly shows the filling defect and is the confirmatory test of choice in a non pregnant patient with normal renal function.
why_wrong_block:
A. D-dimer is sensitive but not specific; a negative result rules out PE in low probability patients, but a positive result cannot establish the diagnosis.
B. Echocardiography shows only indirect signs (RV strain) and is used at the bedside in unstable patients; it does not confirm PE.
D. V/Q scan is the alternative when CT contrast is contraindicated (renal impairment, contrast allergy) or often in pregnancy; it is not first choice here.
key_concept:
PE confirmation = CT pulmonary angiography; D-dimer only rules out in low probability.
  • Risk factors: OCP, surgery, immobilization, pregnancy or postpartum, malignancy
  • Low pretest probability: D-dimer; negative stops the workup
  • High probability or positive D-dimer: CTPA
  • Contrast contraindicated or pregnancy: V/Q scan (leg compression US may come first)
  • Unstable: bedside echo for RV strain
exam_pearl: Read the verb: 'establish the diagnosis' is CTPA; 'rule out in low probability' is D-dimer.

stem: Case presenting with MI and history of hemorrhagic stroke 10 years ago, the current center does not have PCI:
OptA: refer to other hospital with pci
OptD: give asprin, clopidogril, nitrates and heparin
why_right: A history of hemorrhagic stroke at any time is an absolute contraindication to fibrinolysis, so the only safe reperfusion option for this MI is primary PCI. Because the current center does not have PCI, the patient must be transferred urgently to a PCI-capable hospital.
why_wrong_block:
B. Streptokinase is a fibrinolytic; any prior intracranial hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication, however long ago. It would be the choice only when PCI cannot be reached in time and there is no contraindication.
C. tPA is still a fibrinolytic and is equally contraindicated after hemorrhagic stroke; omitting antiplatelets does not remove the intracranial bleeding risk.
D. Aspirin, clopidogrel, nitrates and heparin are adjunctive therapy given alongside reperfusion, not a substitute for it in STEMI. This would be the main treatment for NSTEMI/unstable angina.
key_concept:
STEMI reperfusion: primary PCI is first line; fibrinolysis only if PCI not achievable in time and no contraindication.
  • Absolute contraindications to fibrinolysis: any prior intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke within 3 months, intracranial neoplasm or AV malformation, active bleeding, suspected aortic dissection
  • Contraindicated + no PCI on site: transfer for PCI
  • Adjuncts (antiplatelets, anticoagulant) accompany reperfusion
exam_pearl: Hemorrhagic stroke is a lifelong contraindication; ischemic stroke is only time-limited (within 3 months).

stem: Long term GERD, developed intermittent dysphagia to solid + weight loss Best investigation?
why_right: Long-term GERD with new dysphagia to solids and weight loss are alarm features that raise concern for peptic stricture, Barrett's esophagus or esophageal adenocarcinoma. Alarm features mandate upper endoscopy (EGD), which visualises the mucosa and allows biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Option text not recalled; any alternative listed here would not replace endoscopy when alarm features are present.
C. Manometry is for motility disorders (e.g. achalasia: dysphagia to solids AND liquids) after structural causes are excluded by endoscopy, or before antireflux surgery.
D. Ambulatory pH monitoring is used for refractory GERD with a normal endoscopy, to confirm that reflux causes the symptoms; it cannot detect a stricture or tumour.
key_concept:
GERD with alarm features = endoscopy first.
  • Alarm features: dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, GI bleeding / anemia, persistent vomiting
  • Typical GERD, no alarm features: empirical PPI
  • Refractory GERD: endoscopy; if normal, 24 h pH monitoring
  • Liquids and solids dysphagia from onset: barium swallow then manometry
exam_pearl: Solid-only progressive dysphagia + weight loss = mechanical lesion, scope it; solids and liquids together = motility disorder.

stem: A case of a man traveled to Indonesia & Thailand 1 yr ago Now complain of chronic foul smelling diarrhea for 6 months!! No abdominal pain !!! CBC: ↓ Hb, ↑ MCV = Macrocytic Anemia Tongue exam was showing thick tongue (something like this) What's the diagnosis?
why_right: Chronic malabsorptive diarrhea after a stay in the tropics (Indonesia and Thailand), with macrocytic anemia and a smooth, abnormal tongue (glossitis), is the classic picture of tropical sprue. Mucosal injury of the small bowel causes folate and later B12 malabsorption, giving megaloblastic anemia; treatment is folic acid plus tetracycline.
why_wrong_block:
A. Whipple disease affects mainly middle-aged men with diarrhea plus arthralgia, weight loss, lymphadenopathy or neurological signs; diagnosis is PAS-positive macrophages on duodenal biopsy. No travel link.
C. Celiac disease is triggered by gluten, not travel; it typically causes iron deficiency (microcytic) anemia, with positive tTG IgA and villous atrophy, and improves on a gluten-free diet.
D. SIBO occurs with predisposing anatomy or motility problems (blind loop, prior surgery, diabetes, scleroderma); it causes B12 deficiency but folate is usually normal or high. No such risk factor here.
key_concept:
Travel to tropics + chronic diarrhea + megaloblastic anemia = tropical sprue.
  • Tropical sprue: folate then B12 deficiency; treat folic acid + tetracycline
  • Celiac: gluten, iron deficiency, tTG IgA
  • Whipple: arthralgia, neuro signs, PAS+ macrophages
  • SIBO: predisposing anatomy, low B12, normal/high folate
  • Crohn's ileal: B12 deficiency with abdominal pain
exam_pearl: The travel history is the decisive clue; without it, macrocytic anemia with diarrhea points to ileal disease or celiac.

stem: Old Patient w/ knee arthritis and high WBC, Aspiration is negative for Crystal Culture is pending What to do?
why_right: An inflamed knee with high WBC and aspirate negative for crystals must be treated as septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Once the joint has been aspirated and the sample sent, empirical antibiotics start immediately without waiting for the pending culture, because delay destroys cartilage quickly.
why_wrong_block:
A. NSAIDs relieve pain in crystal arthritis or osteoarthritis but do not treat infection and may mask fever; they are wrong as sole management while sepsis is possible.
B. Steroids (especially intra-articular) are contraindicated until infection is excluded; they are used for gout or pseudogout only after crystals are found and culture is negative.
key_concept:
Hot swollen joint: aspirate first, then empirical IV antibiotics if septic arthritis is possible.
  • Synovial WBC very high (tens of thousands), neutrophil predominant: septic until proven otherwise
  • Negative-birefringent needles: gout; positive-birefringent rhomboids: pseudogout
  • Crystals do not exclude coexisting infection
  • Adjust antibiotics to Gram stain and culture; joint washout if needed
exam_pearl: 'Culture pending' is the cue: never wait for it, and never inject steroid into a possibly infected joint.

stem: A case telling you the Hb electrophoresis showing: ↑↑↑ HbA2 Dx ?
why_right: A raised HbA2 on hemoglobin electrophoresis is the hallmark of beta thalassemia, typically beta thalassemia trait (minor). Reduced beta-chain production leaves spare alpha chains to pair with delta chains, raising HbA2 (α2δ2) above about 3.5%.
why_wrong_block: B. Sickle cell anemia shows predominant HbS with absent HbA and raised HbF; HbA2 is normal. A raised HbA2 with HbS would point to sickle beta thalassemia instead.
key_concept:
Read electrophoresis by the abnormal fraction.
  • Beta thal trait: HbA2 raised (about 3.5 to 7%), HbF normal, mild microcytic anemia
  • Beta thal major: HbA absent, HbF markedly raised, transfusion dependent
  • Sickle cell disease: HbS predominant, HbA absent, HbA2 normal
  • Sickle cell trait: HbS under 50% with HbA present
  • Alpha thal: HbA2 normal or low; HbH in HbH disease
exam_pearl: Coexisting iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask beta thal trait; replete iron and repeat.

stem: A 19-year-old otherwise healthy man presents to the emergency department with gradually worsening right hypochondral pain and generalized fatigue. Examination: Conjunctival pallor and right-upper-quadrant tenderness. Laboratory findings: Hemoglobin: 113 g/L; Haptoglobin: low; LDH: mildly elevated; Reticulocyte count: 2.2%; Coombs (direct antiglobulin) test: not provided. Ultrasound: Gallbladder contains a 2.2-cm gallstone with clear acoustic shadow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 19-year-old otherwise healthy man with anemia, hemolysis markers (low haptoglobin, mildly raised LDH; reticulocytes 2.2%, only borderline) and a 2.2 cm gallstone at a young age points to chronic inherited hemolysis producing pigment stones. Hereditary spherocytosis is the classic membrane defect presenting this way; it is confirmed by spherocytes on smear, a negative Coombs test and osmotic fragility or EMA binding testing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia is acquired, usually acute, and needs a positive Coombs test, which is not provided; it also shows spherocytes, so the Coombs test is what separates it from hereditary spherocytosis.
C. Sickle cell disease also causes pigment gallstones, but it presents from childhood with painful vaso-occlusive crises and more severe anemia; this patient is described as otherwise healthy.
D. DIC occurs in critically ill patients (sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe) with bleeding, thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT and schistocytes; it does not cause gallstones.
key_concept:
Young patient + gallstones + hemolysis = chronic hemolytic anemia (pigment stones).
  • Hemolysis markers: low haptoglobin, high LDH, high indirect bilirubin, high reticulocytes
  • Spherocytes: hereditary spherocytosis vs warm AIHA, separated by Coombs
  • HS tests: osmotic fragility, confirm with EMA binding
  • HS features: splenomegaly, raised MCHC, family history
  • Severe HS: splenectomy (with cholecystectomy if stones)
exam_pearl: If the Coombs test is positive, the same picture becomes warm AIHA.

stem: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus is currently taking the maximum tolerated dose of a statin for dyslipidemia. His recent lipid profile shows LDL slight elevated. What is the most appropriate next step in addition of lifestyle modification?
OptB: Add ezetimibe to the current statin therapy
OptC: Switch to a lower dose of statin and monitor
highlight_terms_source: maximum tolerated dose of a statin
why_right: He is diabetic, so high cardiovascular risk, and his LDL remains above target despite the maximum tolerated dose of a statin. The next step, alongside lifestyle modification, is to add ezetimibe, which further lowers LDL and has outcome benefit when combined with a statin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fibrates mainly lower triglycerides; they are added for severe hypertriglyceridemia, not to replace a statin for raised LDL. Stopping the statin removes the proven cardiovascular benefit.
C. Lowering the statin dose makes LDL worse; it is done only for intolerable side effects, which he does not have.
D. Continuing unchanged is right only when LDL is at target; here it remains elevated in a high-risk diabetic.
key_concept:
LDL above target on maximum tolerated statin: add ezetimibe.
  • Step 1: high-intensity statin + lifestyle
  • Step 2: add ezetimibe
  • Step 3: PCSK9 inhibitor if still above target in very high risk
  • Severe hypertriglyceridemia: fibrate
  • Statin intolerance: lower dose or alternative statin plus non-statin
exam_pearl: 'Maximum tolerated dose' tells you the statin cannot be escalated, so a non-statin add-on is next.

stem: Patient on 3 day of chemotherapy suddenly found arrested, code blue done and shifted to the ICU. What is the cause of sudden event?
why_right: A sudden arrest on day 3 of chemotherapy points to a cardiac rhythm catastrophe. This is the classic window for tumor lysis syndrome, where hyperkalemia (with hypocalcemia) triggers ventricular arrhythmia or asystole, and several chemotherapy agents are directly arrhythmogenic or cause coronary vasospasm. Sudden collapse without a prodrome is the hallmark of a primary arrhythmic arrest.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sepsis (neutropenic) usually builds over hours with fever, rigors and hypotension, and neutropenia typically appears later in the cycle than day 3; it is right when a febrile neutropenic patient deteriorates progressively.
C. Pulmonary embolism is a real risk in active cancer on chemotherapy and a massive PE can cause sudden arrest (often PEA), but the stem gives no immobility, leg swelling, dyspnea or hypoxia to point to it; it is right when those clues are given.
D. Acute stroke presents with focal neurological deficit or reduced consciousness, not primary cardiac arrest; it is right when the stem describes hemiparesis, aphasia or facial droop.
key_concept:
Sudden collapse early after chemotherapy = think arrhythmia (tumor lysis or drug cardiotoxicity).
  • Tumor lysis: high K, high phosphate, high uric acid, low Ca, AKI
  • Timing: typically within the first days of starting therapy
  • Hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, wide QRS, VF or asystole
  • Febrile neutropenia: gradual septic picture, later in the cycle
  • PE: dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, DVT signs first
exam_pearl: "Suddenly found arrested" with no prodrome = rhythm problem; a prodrome of fever or dyspnea would push you to sepsis or PE.

stem: Patient presented with dyspnea due to community acquired pneumonia, the patient unable to complete sentence. pH was 7.1 with hypercapnia and hypoxia. What is the management?
highlight_terms_source: pH was 7.1 with hypercapnia and hypoxia
why_right: This patient has acute hypercapnic and hypoxemic respiratory failure from pneumonia: he is "unable to complete sentences" and the pH is 7.1. Severe respiratory acidosis with exhaustion means the respiratory muscles are failing, so the airway should be secured with a controlled (elective) intubation and mechanical ventilation before he arrests, rather than in a crash setting.
why_wrong_block:
B. BiPAP is mainly for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations or cardiogenic pulmonary edema in a patient who can protect the airway; in pneumonia with severe acidosis it often fails and delays intubation, and 100% oxygen is not the aim of NIV.
C. IV bicarbonate does not treat respiratory acidosis; the fix is ventilation to clear CO2, and bicarbonate can even raise CO2. It has a role in severe metabolic acidosis such as some toxic ingestions.
key_concept:
Respiratory failure with severe acidosis or exhaustion = intubate.
  • Cannot complete sentences, cyanosis, drowsiness = tiring patient
  • Rising PaCO2 with low pH = ventilatory failure
  • NIV: COPD hypercapnia or cardiogenic edema, alert cooperative patient
  • NIV in pneumonia: high failure rate, do not delay intubation
  • Respiratory acidosis is treated with ventilation, not bicarbonate
exam_pearl: A low pH with high CO2 in a non-COPD patient who is exhausted is an airway decision, not an NIV trial.

stem: Patient did Hip arthroplasty. Developed AMS. Was on N5W (no mention on the amount of IVF given). Serum Na: 125, Serum osmolarity: 266, Urine Na: was mildly high. What's the Dx? No mention of volume status!!!
key_concept:
Hyponatremia: check serum osmolality, then volume status, then urine Na.
  • Low osmolality + euvolemia + raised urine Na = SIADH (post-op is a classic setting)
  • Low osmolality + hypovolemia + raised urine Na = renal loss: diuretics, cerebral salt wasting
  • Low osmolality + hypovolemia + low urine Na = GI loss
  • Hypervolemia = heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
  • Dilute urine = water overload or primary polydipsia
  • DI = high Na and high serum osmolality
exam_pearl: Decide by volume status and urine: euvolemic with concentrated urine = SIADH, hypovolemic with a brain insult = cerebral salt wasting, maximally dilute urine after large free water = fluid induced, high Na = DI.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Looong stem with many investigations of SLE with three months hx of SOB, raised JVP, LLO and crepitation. Diagnosis
key_concept:
Raised JVP + edema + ascites in SLE = think pericardium first.
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Constrictive pericarditis.
  • Pericarditis is the most common cardiac manifestation of SLE
  • Constriction: Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, right heart failure picture
  • Liver failure: low JVP, jaundice, coagulopathy, encephalopathy
  • Renal failure: proteinuria, active sediment, rising creatinine
exam_pearl: JVP separates the options: a high JVP puts the cause above the liver and kidney.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Similar recall shown as 1847 (screenshot) with answer A. Pericarditis.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: SLE pt has LL edema, raised JVP, shifting dullness, no chest pain no SOB. Here labs: High ALT&AST, High creatinine. And there were other labs like albumin and urea maybe. What does she have?
highlight_terms_source: LL edema, raised JVP, shifting dullness
why_right: An SLE patient with leg edema, raised JVP and shifting dullness has a right-sided heart failure picture. SLE commonly involves the pericardium, and chronic serositis can lead to constrictive pericarditis, which causes systemic venous congestion. The raised ALT/AST and creatinine reflect congestive hepatopathy and reduced renal perfusion rather than primary organ failure.
why_wrong_block:
B. Liver failure can cause ascites and edema, but it does not raise the JVP; the mild transaminase rise here fits hepatic congestion. It is right with jaundice, coagulopathy and encephalopathy and a normal or low JVP.
C. Kidney failure (lupus nephritis) would need proteinuria or active sediment and a marked creatinine rise; the raised JVP with ascites is better explained by a cardiac cause, with the creatinine rise secondary to congestion.
key_concept:
SLE + raised JVP + ascites + leg edema = constrictive pericarditis.
  • Pericarditis is the most common cardiac manifestation of SLE
  • Kussmaul sign (JVP rises on inspiration)
  • Pericardial knock: early diastolic sound, no murmur or gallop
  • Mild ALT/AST and creatinine rise = congestion
  • Raised JVP excludes isolated liver or kidney disease as the cause
exam_pearl: Ascites with a raised JVP is a heart problem; ascites with a normal JVP is a liver problem.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot highlights A (Pericarditis) and gives answer line 'A'.

stem: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus for 2 years on hydroxychloroquine 200 mg/day, prednisone 5 mg/day, and azathioprine 100 mg/day presented to the Emergency Room with sudden onset of lower limb weakness and urinary incontinence. Examination revealed she has paraplegia and hyperreflexia (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate test to be done immediately?
OptD: Lumbar puncture, MRI, MRA, and MRV of the brain
highlight_terms_source: lower limb weakness and urinary incontinence
why_right: Sudden paraplegia with hyperreflexia and urinary incontinence is an upper motor neuron lesion of both legs plus sphincter loss, which localizes to the spinal cord, not the brain. In SLE this is transverse myelitis until proven otherwise, so the immediate work-up is MRI of the spinal cord plus lumbar puncture for CSF inflammation or infection (she is immunosuppressed). Image first so a compressive lesion is not missed before LP.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lumbar puncture, MRI brain: wrong level; a brain lesion would not usually give isolated bilateral leg weakness with sphincter loss. Right when there are seizures, psychosis, cognitive change or focal hemispheric signs (neuropsychiatric lupus).
B. Lumbar puncture, CT brain: wrong site and CT cannot image the cord. CT brain is the quick test before LP when a raised ICP or mass is suspected in a confused patient.
D. Lumbar puncture, MRI, MRA, and MRV of the brain: vascular brain imaging looks for stroke or cerebral venous thrombosis (e.g. antiphospholipid syndrome); it does not evaluate a cord lesion.
key_concept:
Localize first, then image the right level.
  • Paraplegia + sensory level/sphincter loss + UMN signs = spinal cord
  • SLE + acute myelopathy = transverse myelitis: MRI spine + LP
  • Image before LP to exclude a mass or raised pressure
  • Neuropsychiatric lupus treatment: high-dose steroid + cyclophosphamide
exam_pearl: Bladder involvement with both legs weak points to the cord: pick the option that images the spine, not the brain.

stem: A 43-year-old man comes to the clinic for a follow-up. He has been recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and has been following a plan of lifestyle measures to improve his diet and increase his level of exercise (see lab result). Blood pressure 129/80 mmHg, BMI 32 kg/m2. Test Result Normal Values: HA1C 6.9 4.7-5.6 %. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option now?
why_right: He was recently diagnosed and has already completed a lifestyle plan, yet his HbA1c is still 6.9% with BMI 32. After a 3 to 6 month lifestyle trial, an HbA1c still above 6.5% means lifestyle alone has failed, so metformin is started: it is the first line drug, weight neutral, does not cause hypoglycemia, and suits obese patients.
why_wrong_block:
A. Insulin: started when HbA1c is very high (above 10%) or the patient is catabolic/symptomatic; not for an HbA1c of 6.9%.
C. Sulphonylurea: a second line add on (or for intolerance to metformin); causes weight gain and hypoglycemia, a poor first choice in obesity.
D. Further diet and exercise: appropriate as the first trial at diagnosis, but he has already done this and is still above target, so drug therapy is now needed.
key_concept:
T2DM first step by HbA1c.
  • Below 7.5% at diagnosis: lifestyle for 3 to 6 months, then metformin if HbA1c still above 6.5%
  • 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle + metformin
  • Above 10% or symptomatic catabolism: insulin
  • Metformin avoided if eGFR below 30
  • Usual long term target: HbA1c below 7%
exam_pearl: The lead-in word 'now' after a completed lifestyle trial means escalate to metformin, not more lifestyle.

stem: A 40-year-old man presented with several months history of dyspepsia. He denies any history of dysphagia, vomiting, or weight lost. He has no significant past medical history and not on any medications. He received helicopter pylori eradication (PPI standard dose, clarithromycin 500mg, and amoxil 1g bid for 10 days) with partial response. Basic routine lab was normal (see reports). Endoscopy: Showed gastric erosions. Biopsy: Showed h pylori organism. Which of the following is the best treatment regimen?
OptA: Repeat the same regimen for a longer duration 14 days
OptB: PPI, nitromidazole 500mg bid, doxacyclin 100mg qid for 14 days
OptC: PPI, levofloxacin 500mg gid, amoxil 1 g bid, nitromidazole 500mg bid for 14 days
OptD: PPI, bismuthsubcitrate 300mg qid, tertacycline 500mg id , metronidazole 500mg tid for 14 days
why_right: He received standard clarithromycin based triple therapy, had only a partial response, and a biopsy still shows H. pylori: this is eradication failure. The next regimen should avoid clarithromycin (likely resistance), and bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole for 14 days) is the standard rescue option.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeating the same regimen longer: clarithromycin resistance is the likely reason for failure, so reusing it is not recommended.
B. PPI + metronidazole + doxycycline without bismuth: not a validated eradication regimen; doxycycline is not a substitute for tetracycline here.
C. Levofloxacin based therapy is an alternative rescue (classically PPI + levofloxacin + amoxicillin), but this listed four drug combination is non standard, and bismuth quadruple is the preferred choice offered.
key_concept:
H. pylori treatment ladder.
  • First line: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole if penicillin allergic)
  • Failure: bismuth quadruple (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole) for 14 days
  • Alternative rescue: levofloxacin based triple
  • Confirm eradication: urea breath or stool antigen test, off PPI
exam_pearl: After clarithromycin triple therapy fails, never repeat clarithromycin; switch to bismuth quadruple.

stem: A 40-year-old man with Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease presents to the general physician with 3-month history of intermittent retrosternal burning pain, worse on bending, nausea, regurgitation with an unpleasant taste in the mouth, and a nocturnal cough. The patient has been using over the counter antacids with no relief. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
highlight_terms_source: over the counter antacids with no relief
why_right: Known GERD with 3 months of typical (retrosternal burning worse on bending, regurgitation) and atypical (nocturnal cough) symptoms that failed over the counter antacids needs effective acid suppression. A PPI is the mainstay of GERD treatment and is the most appropriate course now, with lifestyle advice alongside.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgery (fundoplication): reserved for GERD refractory to optimal PPI therapy or with complications; he has not had a PPI yet.
B. Antibiotic: used for H. pylori eradication in peptic ulcer or gastritis, not for reflux symptoms.
C. Lifestyle modification: part of initial management, but alone it is insufficient for persistent symptoms already unresponsive to antacids.
key_concept:
GERD ladder.
  • Typical: heartburn, regurgitation; atypical: nocturnal cough, hoarseness
  • Start: lifestyle advice ± antacids
  • Persistent symptoms: PPI
  • Alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, age above 60, bleeding): endoscopy
  • Refractory to PPI: investigate, then consider fundoplication
exam_pearl: 'Lifestyle modification' is the initial answer only when no treatment has been tried; after failed antacids pick the PPI.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, bloating and weight loss. Physical examination is unremarkable except for BMI 18% (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values: Hb 90 130-170 g/L (Male), 120-160 g/L (Female); MCV 70 80-95 fl; Calcium 2.05 2.15-2.62 mol/L; Phosphate, inorganic 0.79 0.82-1.51 mmol/L; Tissue transglutaminase antibody: Positive. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: Malabsorption features (abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, low BMI), microcytic anemia (Hb 90, MCV 70) from iron malabsorption, low calcium and phosphate, and a positive tissue transglutaminase antibody indicate celiac disease. The treatment is a lifelong strict gluten free diet.
why_wrong_block:
A. Glucocorticoids: used in refractory celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease flares, not as first line for celiac disease.
C. Metronidazole: treats giardiasis, C. difficile or small bowel bacterial overgrowth; serology here points to celiac disease.
D. Ciprofloxacin: for bacterial enteric infections such as traveller's diarrhea; a chronic malabsorptive picture with positive tTG is not infective.
key_concept:
Celiac disease.
  • Clues: diarrhea/bloating, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, low calcium/vitamin D
  • Screen: anti tTG IgA (check total IgA)
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) while on gluten
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten free diet
  • Follow compliance: falling tTG titre
exam_pearl: Iron deficiency anemia in a young adult with no blood loss plus malabsorption = think celiac.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to Emergency Department with altered sensorium. He was recently diagnosed to have inoperable small cell carcinoma of the lung. On examination, he is euvolemic (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 76 /min. Test Result Normal Values: Sodium 115 134-146 mmol/L; Potassium 3.8 3.5-5.1 mmol/L; Urea 4.3 2.75-7.4 mmol/L; Creatinine 76 44-115 mol/L. Which of the following is the best initial management?
highlight_terms_source: small cell carcinoma of the lung
why_right: Small cell lung cancer, euvolemia and Na 115 point to SIADH, but the decisive clue is altered sensorium: this is severe symptomatic hyponatremia. The best initial management is hypertonic (3%) saline to raise sodium promptly, with a limited rate of correction to avoid osmotic demyelination; fluid restriction is for asymptomatic SIADH.
why_wrong_block:
A. 5% dextrose: free water once the glucose is metabolized, which would lower sodium further and worsen cerebral edema.
B. Normal saline: correct for hypovolemic hyponatremia; in SIADH the salt is excreted and water retained, so sodium may fall further.
D. Half normal saline: hypotonic, so it worsens hyponatremia; used in hypernatremia or after initial resuscitation in DKA.
key_concept:
Hyponatremia by volume status and symptoms.
  • Severe symptoms (confusion, seizures, coma): hypertonic 3% saline
  • Hypovolemic: 0.9% saline
  • Euvolemic (SIADH) without severe symptoms: fluid restriction
  • Hypervolemic: fluid restriction + loop diuretic
  • Correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination
exam_pearl: Symptoms trump cause: SIADH is treated with fluid restriction, unless the patient is neurologically symptomatic.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of breathlessness. He has been smoking all his adult life, he smokes 10-15 cigarettes per day. On examination, he has lost the nail fold angle of his fingers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Loss of the nail fold angle is finger clubbing. In a lifelong smoker with 6 months of breathlessness, new clubbing should be assumed to be bronchial carcinoma until proven otherwise, because COPD and asthma never cause clubbing and aspergillosis does not typically present this way.
why_wrong_block:
A. COPD: the commonest cause of breathlessness in smokers, but it does not cause clubbing; clubbing in a COPD patient should prompt a search for lung cancer.
C. Aspergillosis: ABPA presents in asthmatics with wheeze and eosinophilia, aspergilloma with hemoptysis in an old cavity; clubbing is not the key feature.
D. Asthma: episodic wheeze and cough with atopy, usually starting younger; it never causes clubbing.
key_concept:
Clubbing = look for a cause; it is never COPD or asthma alone.
  • Lung: bronchial carcinoma, bronchiectasis, lung abscess/empyema, cystic fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis
  • Cardiac: cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis
  • GI: inflammatory bowel disease, cirrhosis, celiac disease
exam_pearl: Smoker + breathlessness alone = COPD; smoker + clubbing = bronchial carcinoma.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of 20-pack-year smoking presents with exertional dyspnea and productive cough for 3 months. He had similar attack last year. On examination, he has central cyanosis and expiratory wheeze on lung auscultation (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: ABG HCO3- 36 22-28 mmol/L; ABG PCO2 7.7 4.7-6.0 kPa; pH 7.35 7.36-7.45; ABG PO2 8.4 10.6-14.2 kPa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: "Productive cough for 3 months" with a "similar attack last year" in a 20 pack-year smoker is the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis (productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years). Central cyanosis plus wheeze is the "blue bloater" picture, and the ABG shows CO2 retention (PCO2 7.7 kPa) with a raised HCO3 of 36 and near-normal pH 7.35: a chronic, metabolically compensated respiratory acidosis typical of COPD.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asthma is episodic and reversible, usually starts younger, and does not produce chronic CO2 retention with a compensatory high bicarbonate. Right when: variable wheeze with triggers and a big bronchodilator response.
C. PE is acute and causes hypoxia with LOW PCO2 from hyperventilation, not a 3 month productive cough recurring yearly. Right when: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, DVT risk.
D. Interstitial fibrosis gives a dry cough, fine "Velcro" inspiratory crackles, clubbing and a restrictive pattern with type 1 failure (normal or low PCO2), not wheeze and CO2 retention.
key_concept:
Smoker + productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years = chronic bronchitis.
  • High PCO2 + high HCO3 + near-normal pH = chronic compensated respiratory acidosis (CO2 retainer)
  • Blue bloater: cyanosis, cough, CO2 retention (chronic bronchitis)
  • PE: low PCO2
  • ILD: dry cough, Velcro crackles, restrictive, type 1 failure
exam_pearl: A raised HCO3 with a high PCO2 tells you the CO2 retention is chronic: think COPD, not an acute event.

stem: A 60-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for cardiac risk assessment. He is asymptomatic and physically active. He has never smoked. He has no chronic health issues and takes no medications. His physical examinations are normal. Cardiovascular risk calculation using the Pooled Cohort Equations predicts a 6.5% risk of a myocardial infarction in the next 10 years that indicate an intermediate risk of myocardial infarction. Which of the following investigations should be done next?
why_right: The patient is "asymptomatic" and the Pooled Cohort Equations place him at "intermediate risk", so the question is how to refine his risk to decide on a statin, not how to look for ischemia. High-sensitivity CRP is a risk-enhancing marker that, added to the calculated risk, helps tip the decision toward statin therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coronary CT angiography is anatomic imaging for symptomatic patients with suspected coronary disease, not risk refinement in someone without symptoms.
B. Stress echo looks for inducible ischemia and is indicated for symptoms suggesting angina; it is not a screening test in asymptomatic people.
D. CMR evaluates cardiac structure, function and tissue (cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, viability); it has no role in primary prevention risk refinement.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic + intermediate ASCVD risk: refine risk to guide statin, do not image for ischemia.
  • Risk enhancers: hs-CRP, family history of premature ASCVD, Lp(a), ApoB, ABI, CKD, metabolic syndrome
  • If imaging is used for refinement it is a non-contrast coronary calcium score, not CT angiography
  • Symptoms suggesting ischemia: stress testing or CCTA
exam_pearl: "Asymptomatic" in the stem rules out every ischemia or anatomy test; pick the risk-refining marker.

stem: A 68-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnea and dry cough for 7 days. His medical history is significant for hypertension. Physical examination reveals raised central venous pressure, fine crackles at lung bases and hepatomegaly. His extremity examination reveals bilateral pitting edema. Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% and normal valves. Chest radiograph shows evidence of pulmonary edema (see lab results). Blood pressure 160/85 mmHg, Heart rate 86 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min. Test Result Normal Values: Sodium 140 134-146 mmol/L; Potassium 4 3.5-5.1 mmol/L; Urea 6 2.75-7.4 mmol/L; Creatinine 88 44-115 mol/L; Brain natriuretic peptide 900 0-300 ng/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: Orthopnea, raised CVP, basal crackles, hepatomegaly, pitting edema, pulmonary edema on CXR and BNP 900 mean acute decompensated heart failure with congestion. The preserved EF (60%, normal valves) in a hypertensive man makes it HFpEF, but that does not change the acute step: relieve congestion with a loop diuretic (furosemide).
why_wrong_block:
A. Calcium channel blockers do not relieve fluid overload, and non-dihydropyridines are negatively inotropic. They may help long-term BP control, not acute congestion.
B. Beta-blockers are not started during acute decompensation; they are introduced once the patient is euvolemic and stable (mainly for HFrEF).
C. Spironolactone is long-term prognostic therapy, with a weak and slow diuretic effect; it is not the immediate treatment for pulmonary edema.
key_concept:
ADHF with congestion: IV loop diuretic first, regardless of EF.
  • Clues: orthopnea, raised JVP, crackles, edema, hepatomegaly, high BNP
  • HFpEF: diuretics for congestion + control BP and comorbidities
  • Do not START beta-blockers in decompensation
  • MRA and beta-blockers = chronic prognostic therapy
exam_pearl: A normal EF does not exclude heart failure: congestion signs plus high BNP still mean furosemide.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presented to the clinic with 2-months history of polyarthralgia, skin rash, mucosal ulcers and fatigue. Her clinical examinations revealed malar rash over her face and active arthritis at several joints (see lab results). Hb 100 (130-170 g/L male; 120-160 g/L female); Platelets count 100 (150-400 x 10^9/L); WBC 3 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L); ESR 35; Lupus anticoagulant positive (negative); Urea 5; Creatinine 78; C-reactive peptide 5 (<8.2 mg/L); Complement C3 0.3 (0.7-1.5 g/L); Complement C4 0.13 (0.15-0.45 g/L). Which of the following test obtained at this visit is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is ANA. The young woman has a classic SLE picture: malar rash, mucosal ulcers, arthritis, pancytopenia, low C3/C4 and a positive lupus anticoagulant. ANA is positive in nearly all SLE patients, so it is the test used to establish the autoimmune basis; a negative ANA practically excludes SLE.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-Ro (SSA) is linked to Sjögren syndrome, subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus/congenital heart block; it is not the test that confirms systemic lupus.
C. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and tracks disease activity and nephritis, but it is negative in a sizeable share of patients, so it cannot exclude lupus; this recall keys the sensitive test, ANA.
D. Anti-RNP confirms mixed connective tissue disease (SLE features overlapping with myositis, Raynaud, scleroderma); there is no myositis or overlap here.
key_concept:
SLE antibodies: ANA most sensitive, anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA most specific.
  • ANA: most sensitive, screening; negative ANA practically excludes SLE
  • Anti-Sm: most specific
  • Anti-dsDNA: specific, activity and nephritis
  • Low C3/C4: activity, nephritis
  • Anti-histone: drug-induced lupus
  • Anti-Ro/La: neonatal lupus, Sjögren
exam_pearl: "Most sensitive / screening" = ANA; "most specific" = anti-Sm (then anti-dsDNA); SLE plus myositis overlap = anti-RNP.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed version: 'Long case with classic presentation of SLE. Asking what is most important initial serology test? A- Anti-ccp, B- ANA, B- Anti-dsDna, C- Antiphospholipid. Answer: B (ANA).' Fuller screenshot version (top of next page) marks ** B. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA).

stem: Radiation exposure After 2 wks , abdominal pain loss of appetite and genralize fatigue
why_right: After significant radiation exposure the bone marrow is the most radiosensitive organ, and the hematopoietic syndrome declares itself after a latent period, with counts falling over the following weeks. Symptoms appearing "after 2 wks" such as generalized fatigue, anorexia and abdominal discomfort fit bone marrow destruction (anemia, neutropenia with infection, thrombocytopenia), rather than an immediate or a late effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anaphylactic shock is an immediate IgE-mediated reaction to an allergen (minutes), with hypotension, urticaria and bronchospasm; radiation does not cause it and the timing is 2 weeks.
B. Radiation-induced malignancy (leukemia, thyroid, solid tumors) is a late effect appearing years later, not 2 weeks after exposure.
key_concept:
Acute radiation syndrome: prodrome, latent phase, then organ syndrome by dose.
  • Hematopoietic: lowest dose; pancytopenia over weeks (fatigue, infection, bleeding)
  • Gastrointestinal: higher dose; vomiting, diarrhea, GI bleeding
  • Neurovascular: very high dose; rapid collapse, fatal
  • Malignancy: late effect, years later
exam_pearl: Timing decides: minutes = allergy, weeks = marrow failure, years = cancer.

stem: Pt with left-sided sensorineural hearing loss and left-sided facial weakness
why_right: The labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery usually arises from the AICA, and the AICA also supplies the lateral inferior pons where the facial nucleus and nerve lie. So an AICA infarct gives ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss plus ipsilateral facial weakness (CN VIII + CN VII), often with vertigo and ataxia, exactly the "left-sided hearing loss and left-sided facial weakness" here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Not a standard posterior circulation vessel; if the superior cerebellar artery is intended, it causes ipsilateral limb ataxia and contralateral pain and temperature loss, without hearing loss or facial palsy.
B. MCA stroke gives CONTRALATERAL face and arm weakness (upper motor neuron, forehead spared), sensory loss and aphasia or neglect; it does not cause hearing loss.
key_concept:
Brainstem strokes: ipsilateral cranial nerve signs + crossed long tract signs.
  • AICA (lateral pontine): ipsilateral deafness (CN VIII) + facial palsy (CN VII), vertigo, ataxia
  • PICA (lateral medullary, Wallenberg): dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, Horner
  • SCA: ipsilateral ataxia
  • MCA: contralateral face/arm weakness, aphasia
exam_pearl: Hearing loss in a stroke points to AICA, because the labyrinthine artery comes off it.
compiler_note: Compiler note: AICA syndrome responsible for both CN VII and CN VIII palsies. (Screenshot originally numbered 388.)

stem: Adult patient presented with meningitis. No Na mentioned. Most likely causative organism?
why_right: This recall's key is Listeria monocytogenes, which is the organism to name when an adult with meningitis has a Listeria risk factor: age over 50, pregnancy, immunosuppression (steroids, transplant, malignancy), diabetes or alcoholism. The recall has lost most of its stem detail ("No Na mentioned"), so the original question likely contained one of these clues; Listeria is also why ampicillin is added to empirical cover in those groups.
why_wrong_block:
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults overall; it is the answer for a previously well adult without Listeria risk factors.
C. Staphylococcal meningitis follows neurosurgery, shunts, penetrating head trauma or bacteremia from endocarditis, not typical community-acquired meningitis.
D. E. coli is a neonatal meningitis organism (with group B strep and Listeria) or follows neurosurgery; it is not typical in community adults.
key_concept:
Meningitis organism by host:
  • Neonate: group B strep, E. coli, Listeria
  • Adult (most common overall): S. pneumoniae; young adults: also N. meningitidis
  • Over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised, alcoholic: add Listeria (cover with ampicillin)
  • Post-neurosurgery or shunt: Staphylococcus, Gram negatives
exam_pearl: No risk factor in an adult = pneumococcus; age over 50, pregnancy or immunosuppression is what turns the answer to Listeria.

stem: Best antihypertensive medication after TIA?
why_right: For secondary prevention "after TIA" or stroke, BP lowering with an ACE inhibitor (often combined with a thiazide-like diuretic) has trial evidence for reducing recurrent stroke, so ramipril is the preferred choice. ACE inhibitors also protect the kidney and heart in the many TIA patients who have diabetes or vascular disease.
why_wrong_block: A. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol are less effective at preventing stroke than other classes and are not first line for hypertension after TIA; use them when there is another indication (angina, post-MI, HFrEF, rate control in AF).
key_concept:
Antihypertensive choice by indication:
  • After TIA/stroke: ACE inhibitor ± thiazide-like diuretic
  • Diabetes or CKD with proteinuria: ACE inhibitor/ARB
  • Post-MI, angina, HFrEF: beta-blocker added
  • Beta-blockers: weakest for stroke prevention
exam_pearl: Beta-blockers are the trap: good for the heart, poor for stroke prevention.
